name: Safety and Pharmacovigilance
blurb: AI in adverse event detection, case processing, signal management and drug safety governance.
title: Safety and Pharmacovigilance
answer: Pharmacovigilance was one of the first places pharma used AI at scale, because safety case processing is high volume and rule bound. Machine learning now helps extract and triage adverse event reports and spot signals in real world data, and international groups and regulators have set out how such systems should be governed.

reading.body:
Pharmacovigilance adopted AI early because adverse event processing is high volume and rule bound, and regulators now expect these systems to be governed and validated.

The pattern is that safety AI grew from the paperwork outward. Machine learning first learned to extract key case information and identify valid safety cases from historical database content, then moved into triage, literature screening, and signal detection in real world data. Each step targets work that is repetitive and text heavy, which is why language models fit the extraction problem well.

Governance arrived alongside the tools rather than after them. CIOMS Working Group XIV set out how AI tools that influence patient safety should be governed and validated. The FDA and EMA guiding principles of good AI practice explicitly cover pharmacovigilance, and the EMA reflection paper names case management and signal detection among the lifecycle uses regulators expect. The EU AI Act adds a further layer where safety AI falls within its scope.

For a safety team the operating rule is narrow. Use AI to speed intake and triage, keep a qualified person accountable for every case and signal decision, and keep the evidence that each model was validated for its exact task. That is what inspectors will ask for.

What this does not cover is cost, headcount, or measured accuracy. The data names no vendor systems, no error rates, and no deployment counts, so it cannot say how much of the work is automated today or how well any given model performs. It describes the direction of adoption and the shape of the oversight, not the results.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

Baseline workforce understanding of AI capability, limits, and policy: what the tools can do, where they fail, and what the rules are. Under the EU AI Act it is now a legal requirement for providers and deployers, not just good practice.
The European regulation classifying AI systems by risk, with obligations scaled to each tier: prohibited, high-risk, limited, minimal.

siblings.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

explainer:
Pharmacovigilance is the work of detecting, assessing and preventing harm from medicines after they are approved. Companies must collect reports of adverse events from patients, doctors, the literature and other sources, process each report into a structured safety case, report serious cases to regulators within strict deadlines, and look across all the data for new safety signals.

The volume is enormous and growing, and much of the work is repetitive: reading a report, extracting the patient, drug and event, coding them, checking for duplicates and judging whether the case is valid. That is why safety was one of the first areas in pharma to use automation and machine learning at scale. Language models now extract events from free text, screen the scientific literature, translate reports and draft case narratives.

The stakes are what make governance central. A missed report or a missed signal can harm patients and breach legal obligations, so AI in pharmacovigilance is held to standards close to those for other validated systems: tested on realistic data, monitored for drift, and kept under the oversight of qualified people who remain accountable for medical judgements such as seriousness and causality. International guidance from CIOMS, joint FDA and EMA principles and industry work through TransCelerate set out how to do this.

The business case is straightforward: case processing is the largest cost in a safety budget, and automation lets teams keep up with rising volumes without lowering quality.
key_points: Case processing is the largest cost and the first target for automation.
Language models extract events, screen literature and draft narratives.
Missing a case or signal is the critical risk, so tools are tuned for recall.
Qualified people stay accountable for seriousness, causality and signal decisions.
CIOMS, FDA and EMA principles and TransCelerate tools guide governance.
